\noindent{\LARGE\bfseries Birding Coach}\hfill{\small\textcolor{gray}{Tharaka Jayalath · 1 August 2026}}

\vspace{1pt}

\noindent{\large\textcolor{petrol}{Every birding app tells you \textit{where}. This one tells you \textit{when}.}}

\vspace{3pt}
\noindent\textcolor{rulegrey}{\rule{\linewidth}{0.9pt}}

Tell it where you are and which bird you want. It gives back the closest hotspot
and the hours worth going, using next week's forecast and what birders have
actually recorded at those places.

**Log.** People record what they saw, plus how long they birded, how far they
walked, and whether they listed everything they could identify. Those last three
are what other logging apps skip, and they are the ones that matter. Without
them you have a pile of sightings and no way to judge what any one sighting was
worth. The logs also drive a leaderboard, ranked by how many species you found
against what the model expected for your effort. Someone birding an hour a week
can beat someone birding forty.

**Forecast.** Pick a bird, pick a spot. The app lists nearby eBird hotspots
ordered by your chances rather than by how far away they are, then scores every
hour of the coming week. Darker means better odds. Underneath, it breaks down
where the number came from, so you can see that leaving at dawn bought you more
than the weather did.

## Behind it

A penalised logistic model of detection: the chance that someone birding the
way you plan to, there, at that hour, reports the species. One model per
species, 69 of them.

It is fitted on complete eBird checklists, meaning lists where the birder said
they recorded everything they could identify. That matters more than it sounds.
If a species is missing from a complete list, that is a real absence. Without it
you can count sightings but you cannot compute a probability.

Predictors are the checklist's own effort, the hour, the season, the site, and
weather at that site's grid cell for the hours the outing covered. At prediction
time the forecast goes in. The coefficients come from what has already been
recorded.

The penalty is what lets all 192 hotspots carry their own effect. A spot
visited 89 times keeps its own estimate; one visited four times is pulled
toward the county average. Without it, a hotspot where the bird was seen every
single visit produces an infinite coefficient, which cost roughly half the
species when site effects were first added.

Right now it trains on eBird. As people log their own sightings, that feeds a
recalibration layer, and the app can lean more on its own data over time.

## Scope

This runs on Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, which is a data problem rather than
a modelling one. eBird has no bulk endpoint, so getting the denominator costs two
API calls per checklist. That is roughly 4,650 calls for a month of one county,
438,000 for a year of Pennsylvania, and over a million for a month of the whole
country. Going wider means asking eBird for the Basic Dataset instead of
scraping. I still need to work out how to get access to it.
